Austropotamobius torrentium, the stone crayfish, is a relatively small-bodied freshwater decapod with a life history closely tied to cool, well-oxygenated headwater streams. The initial energy content of the egg, estimated from comparisons with related Cherax species, is approximately 70.1 Joules , a value that reflects the large average egg diameter of 2.8 millimeters for this species. Upon hatching, the emerging juvenile possesses a carapace length of roughly 0.34 centimeters , a diminutive size that marks the beginning of a prolonged growth period. Females on Medvednica Mountain in Croatia have been recorded reaching a maximum total length of 9.7 centimeters [Li = 9.7 centimeters], while males in the same population tend to attain a slightly larger ultimate size, with the longest documented male measuring 10.5 centimeters [Li = 10.5 centimeters] in total length. These sizes are consistent with reports from other Central European populations, indicating a moderate degree of sexual dimorphism in this species.

The timing of key reproductive events in Austropotamobius torrentium is strongly influenced by ambient water temperature. At 12 °C [T = 12 °C], females attain sexual maturity at a total body length of approximately 6.0 centimeters [Lp = approximately 6.0 centimeters], and this milestone corresponds to a carapace length at puberty of about 2.6 centimeters [Lp = about 2.6 centimeters], the point at which the pubertal moult typically occurs. The time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 3 years since birth [tp = 3 years since birth] when individuals develop at 12 °C at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. During the breeding season in autumn, a female produces between 50 and 100 eggs per brood [N_R_i = between 50 and 100 eggs per brood] in a single reproductive event each year [F_R_i = single reproductive event each year], leading to a modest annual reproductive output characteristic of a k-selected life history strategy.

The embryonic and early post-embryonic phases are particularly sensitive to temperature, and development proceeds slowly in this stenothermic species. At a constant water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the incubation period from egg deposition to hatching lasts approximately 210 days , a duration that spans the entirety of the winter season. Following eclosion, the newly hatched individuals spend about ten additional days, reaching a full age at birth of about 220 days [ab = about 220 days], at the same temperature of 10 °C attached to the mother's pleopods before they begin their first independent foraging and are considered fully born at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This extended period of maternal association provides crucial protection during the vulnerable transition from lecithotrophic to exogenous feeding, with the young crayfish beginning to feed on live invertebrates soon after their first moult.

Adult body size in Austropotamobius torrentium exhibits notable sexual dimorphism, with males generally attaining greater mass. In the population from Medvednica, Croatia, the ultimate wet weight of females is approximately 40 grams [Wwi = approximately 40 grams], whereas males reach a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of about 70 grams [Wwi = about 70 grams]. These field-recorded masses are somewhat lower than the absolute maximum of 100 grams reported for the species in the Encyclopedia of Life, likely reflecting local environmental constraints such as food availability and stream productivity. In terms of total length at puberty, females become reproductively active at around 6.0 centimeters [Lp = around 6.0 centimeters], though the smallest egg-bearing female documented in a separate Croatian study was 6.42 centimeters long, suggesting that sexual maturation may also be influenced by energetic condition rather than size alone.

Comparative longevity data for related freshwater crayfish indicate a maximum lifespan for Austropotamobius torrentium of roughly 20 years [am = roughly 20 years], an estimate derived from populations at a mean annual water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This extended life expectancy, coupled with a late onset of reproduction—females typically first spawn at approximately 3 years after birth [tp = approximately 3 years after birth] at 12 °C—places the stone crayfish at the slow end of the life-history continuum among Eur at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]opean astacids. The sizable maternal investment per egg of roughly 70.1 Joules  underscores the energy-rich yolk provisioned to each embryo, fed by a large egg diameter averaging 2.8 millimeters. This strategy of producing few, large, energy-rich eggs is consistent with the species' occupancy of stable, low-nutrient headwater environments where competitive interactions with faster-growing crayfish species are minimized.
